abstract_sentences.text: In recent years, there has been growing interest in understanding neural architectures’ ability to learn to execute discrete algorithms, a line of work often referred to as neural algorithmic reasoning.

evidence.anchor: In recent years, there has been growing interest

abstract_sentences.transition: opens the field and names NAR.

abstract_sentences.text: The goal is to integrate algorithmic reasoning capabilities into larger neural pipelines.
Many such architectures are based on (message-passing) graph neural networks (MPNNs), owing to their permutation equivariance and ability to deal with sparsity and variable-sized inputs.

However, much existing work is either largely empirical and lacks formal guarantees or it focuses solely on expressivity, leaving open the question of when and how such architectures generalize beyond a finite training set.
abstract_sentences.transition: sets the gap that the framework answers.

abstract_sentences.text: In this work, we propose a general theoretical framework that characterizes sufficient conditions under which MPNNs can learn an algorithm from a training set of small instances and provably approximate its behavior on inputs of arbitrary size with worst-case guarantees.
abstract_sentences.comparison: finite small instances versus arbitrary-size inputs
abstract_sentences.transition: answers the gap with the central theorem.

abstract_sentences.text: Our framework applies to a broad class of algorithms, including single-source shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, and general dynamic programming problems, such as the 0-1 knapsack problem.

evidence.anchor: single-source shortest paths, minimum spanning trees

abstract_sentences.text: In addition, we establish impossibility results for a wide range of algorithmic tasks, showing that standard MPNNs cannot learn them and derive more expressive MPNN-like architectures that overcome these limitations.

evidence.anchor: impossibility results for a wide range

abstract_sentences.comparison: standard MPNNs versus more expressive variants

abstract_sentences.text: Finally, we refine our analysis for the Bellman–Ford algorithm, yielding substantially smaller required training sets and significantly extending the recent work of Nerem et al. (2025) by allowing for a differentiable regularization loss.

evidence.anchor: allowing for a differentiable regularization loss

abstract_sentences.transition: narrows to the constructive SSSP special case.

abstract_sentences.text: Empirical results largely support our theoretical findings.

abstract_summary.experimental_result_form: Qualified, nonnumeric sentence: empirical results largely support theory.

evidence.anchor: central tool across a wide range

method_moves.problem_addressed: Provides graph, invariant, and norm notation used in the theorem.
Defines node update/aggregation and graph readout in Equation (1)–(2).
Separates expressibility from learnability and uniform size generalization.
Introduces pseudometric, finite cover, certificate, empirical loss, and regularizer.
Connects small regularized loss on a cover to uniform error.
Explains why a computable certificate, rather than true Lipschitz constant, is trained.
Shows a mean-aggregation instance with size-independent truncation error.
Represents K-step SSSP with min aggregation.
Reduces 0-1 knapsack and similar DP problems to shortest paths.
Constructs K+1 Bellman–Ford path examples and weighted differentiable ℓ1 loss.
Contrasts Nerem et al. while stating fixed-depth, one-dimensional aggregation, and scaling costs.
Distinguishes expressivity impossibility from learnability obstruction.
Maps Q1–Q3 to optimization, expressivity, and regularizer claims.

method_analysis.formal_objects: graphs; k-tuple invariants; MPNN class; pseudo-metric; finite cover; certificate Bθ; target f*; empirical/regularized loss; Bellman–Ford path graph; transformed loss.
method_analysis.inputs_outputs: Input is a graph or rooted graph/tuple; outputs are invariant algorithm values/features. The SSSP special case outputs K-step node distances.
method_analysis.objective: General L_emp plus certificate regularizer; SSSP MAE plus layer-weighted differentiable ℓ1 regularizer.
method_analysis.transition_sequence: setup_notation → state_problem → define_component → derive → give_intuition → instantiate_algorithm → contrast_alternative → connect_to_experiment

final_judgment.single_storyline: The paper converts arbitrary-size algorithm learning into a pseudometric/finite-cover/certificate problem, then makes Bellman–Ford a constructive K+1-path special case.
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: Gap, informal theorems, a twofold negative boundary, Q1–Q3, Figure 1–2, Table 1–2, and explicit limitations.
final_judgment.appendix_moves: All formal proofs and constants, Bellman–Ford loss/training construction, counterexamples, topology, hyperparameters, runtime, and additional/deeper-step results; Appendix to main-text page ratio is about 6.9:1.
final_judgment.best_pattern: General theorem → constructive special case → matched experimental question, made legible by Figure 1, Figure 3, and Tables 1–2.
final_judgment.largest_gap: The title reads broadly, but the paper provides conditional sufficient conditions and selected obstructions; general covers may be nonconstructive and gradient-descent convergence is unproved.
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For a size-generalization claim, close the loop among a general condition, a constructible training example, a negative expressivity boundary, and a controlled empirical test.
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: This applies when stable representations, finite-cover structure, bounded-certificate approximation, and supervised losses are available; it does not automatically cover mixed aggregation, unmarked initial conditions, or optimizer convergence.
